name: rebar
description: A personal workout logging app inspired by Hevy.
writeup: Log gym sessions: exercises, sets, weight, and reps. Follow other people and see their finished sessions alongside your own.
Moving over from Hevy? It imports your full history from a CSV export instead of starting from scratch. Backend's ASP.NET Core, Postgres, and Redis; the app itself is Expo React Native.

name: ledgr
description: Ledger and transfer infrastructure for reliable internal money movement.
writeup: Provides account management, double-entry posting, and idempotent transfer orchestration. Every journal post is validated as balanced before persistence.
Handles account lifecycle, settlement netting, and clearing account health checks. Idempotent transfer submission with optional Redis-backed deduplication.

name: hum
description: Identifies songs by listening to a few seconds of audio.
writeup: Like Shazam: record a few seconds of a song and it tells you what it is. Based on a 2003 research paper that figured out how to match audio even in noisy rooms with bad microphones.
Instead of comparing raw sound, it fingerprints pairs of frequency peaks. That's what makes it resilient to background noise and low-quality recordings.

name: backtester
description: Test trading strategies against historical crypto and stock data.
writeup: Grabs past prices from Binance and Yahoo Finance, then runs four strategies against them: EMA crossover, RSI, Bollinger Bands, and buy-and-hold. Every strategy reports the same five metrics, so you can compare apples to apples.
There's a browser dashboard for equity curves, drawdowns, and the full trade log, so you can see exactly where a strategy made or lost money.

name: mapreduce
description: A textbook MapReduce. Run the same job one thread, many cores, or across a cluster.
writeup: Implements Google's MapReduce paper from 2004. Same word-count job runs three ways: sequentially on one thread, parallel across CPU cores, and distributed across a master node and its workers.
The map and reduce logic stays identical in all three. Only the scheduling changes: one thread, then many, then a whole cluster.

name: dozer
description: A lightweight ORM for .NET that maps your classes to database tables.
writeup: Lets you work with database rows as regular C# objects. CRUD operations, a fluent query builder, and schema auto-generated from your classes, no separate mapping files.
Tracks which fields you changed, so an update only touches what actually changed. Fetching the same row twice gives you the same object, not two copies that drift apart.

name: linear-kv
description: A key-value store where every operation happens in strict order.
writeup: An in-memory key-value store on a single node, where one lock ensures operations never overlap. Writes include a request ID, so a retried PUT doesn't apply twice.
Ships with a linearizability checker. It records every operation's timeline and validates it against the consistency claim, instead of just assuming it works.

name: crossdial
description: Checks and cleans up international phone numbers.
writeup: Validates and formats international phone numbers. Works with single numbers or batches, and returns structured errors instead of crashing on the first bad one.
Published to Maven Central. Handles the tedious parts: thread safety, clear error messages, and a list of supported countries so you know what it can actually handle.
